Sailors
SAY-lurz
n. pl. (seamen; in Revelation 18, among the mourners standing afar off from the burning of Babylon)
From sail, Old English segl. At Revelation 18:17 it renders Greek nautes, a seaman — the root of our word nautical.

Biblical Definition

John's vision of the fall of Babylon names three groups of mourners, and the last of them works the water: For in one hour so great riches is come to nought. And every shipmaster, and all the company in ships, and sailors, and as many as trade by sea, stood afar off. Kings, merchants, and then the men who moved the goods. What unites them is not affection for the city but dependence on her trade, and the lament they raise is an accounting: no man buyeth their merchandise any more. They stand afar off for fear of her torment, and they weep for the market.

The phrase in one hour is repeated three times in the chapter, and it is the heart of the warning. The wealth of centuries, the shipping of an empire, the whole apparatus of buying and selling that reached from cinnamon to slaves, and souls of men, is undone inside an hour. James says the same thing to men who plan a year of buying and selling and getting gain, and asks them what their life is — a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away. Scripture does not treat seafaring or trade as evil; the virtuous woman is like the merchants' ships, and the Lord Himself taught from a fishing boat. What it treats as fatal is the confidence that a system of commerce is permanent, and the grief of men who discover in an hour that it was not.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): mariners; seamen; men whose occupation is to navigate ships.

expand to see more

SAILOR, n. A mariner; a seaman; one who follows the seas.

MARINER, n. A seaman or sailor; one whose occupation is to assist in navigating ships.

SHIPMASTER, n. The captain, master or commander of a ship.

MERCHANDISE, n. The objects of commerce; wares, goods, commodities bought and sold.

TRADE, n. In a general sense, the act or business of exchanging commodities by barter or purchase.

Key Scripture

Revelation 18:17 — "For in one hour so great riches is come to nought. And every shipmaster, and all the company in ships, and sailors, and as many as trade by sea, stood afar off,"

Revelation 18:11 — "And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more:"

Revelation 18:19 — "And they cast dust on their heads, and cried, weeping and wailing, saying, Alas, alas, that great city, wherein were made rich all that had ships in the sea by reason of her costliness! for in one hour is she made desolate."

James 4:13 — "Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain:"

Modern Corruption

Revelation 18 is read as a prophecy chart about a future city and not as the standing verdict on every economy that treats permanence as its birthright.

expand to see more

Much energy has been spent identifying Babylon with a particular city on a map, and the identification, whichever is chosen, tends to end the reading. The chapter itself is more interested in the merchandise list, which runs from gold and silk and cinnamon down to beasts, and sheep, and horses, and chariots, and slaves, and souls of men — a trade that has ended by selling people, filed between livestock and luxury goods. That is the indictment. Wherever an economy arrives at the point of pricing human beings, the sailors' lament is already written for it.

The other half of the warning is directed inward, and John states it as a command in the same chapter: Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues. That is not a call to leave a geography but to leave a way of living — to stop measuring a life by its market position. Men who have done so can hear in one hour without terror. The sailors of verse 17 stood afar off and wept because everything they had was in the freight; a Christian whose treasure is elsewhere may work the same ships and lose nothing that matters when they stop sailing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek nautes (G3492), a seaman; kubernetes (G2942), a shipmaster or pilot; emporos (G1713), a merchant.

expand to see more

Greek nautes (G3492) — a sailor, a seaman; from naus, a ship.

Greek kubernetes (G2942) — a steersman, a shipmaster; the root of our word govern.

Greek emporos (G1713) — a merchant, one who travels to trade; the class that weeps first in Revelation 18.

Greek gomos (G1117) — a cargo, a freight; the list that ends with souls of men.

Greek mia hora (G3391 / G5610) — one hour; repeated three times over the fall of the city.

Usage

"“every shipmaster, and all the company in ships, and sailors” — the men who moved the goods."

"“in one hour so great riches is come to nought” — the refrain of the chapter."

"“Alas, alas, that great city” — a lament that is really an accounting."
